title: Linear NeuroPaint: An Efficient Baseline for Cross-Session Neural Alignment and Inpainting
authors: Yao, Y. J.; Xia, J.; Paninski, L.; Miller, K. D.
abstract: Large-scale Neuropixels recordings sample many brain areas, but no single experimental session records every area of interest. NeuroPaint, a transformer-based autoencoder, integrates such recordings by aligning area-specific latent dynamics across sessions and "inpainting" activity in unrecorded areas. Could a linear model, which would be computationally efficient and potentially more interpretable, suffice to achieve this? To address this question, we introduce Linear NeuroPaint, a linear variant of NeuroPaint, and evaluate it on two multi-area Neuropixels datasets. Linear NeuroPaint achieves strong predictive performance on recorded areas, however, it is less accurate than nonlinear models at cross-area inpainting, despite extensive hyperparameter optimization. Moreover, its parameters are not readily interpretable: incomplete cross-session alignment leads parameter-defined neuron clusters to exhibit heterogeneous response profiles. Together, these results show that linear transformations are insufficient for cross-session alignment and cross-area prediction. Nevertheless, Linear NeuroPaint provides a computationally efficient baseline for benchmarking multi-session neural models.

title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
authors: Shao, J.; Chen, M.; Liu, Y.; Sun, J.; Zhang, G.; Yan, Z.-Y.; Lin, H.; Ren, M.; Pei, S.; Peng, J.; Gong, Y.; WANG, S.
abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.

title: An iPSC-based experimental framework for investigating phenotypic variation associated with Jomon ancestry in the present-day Japanese population
authors: Nakamura, Y.; Watanabe, Y.; Tanabe, H.; Hirai, A.; Higashi, K.; Kurokawa, K.; Toyoda, A.; Kato, T.; Tsukahara, M.; Koganebuchi, K.; Hamazaki, Y.; Takebe, T.; Imamura, M.; Ishida, T.; Ohashi, J.; Oota, H.
abstract: Ancestry-related genomic variation may contribute to phenotypic diversity. However, its cellular consequences remain difficult to evaluate. To address this, we developed a human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-based framework for investigating such phenotypes. We used the Japanese population as a model of Jomon-related and continental East Asian ancestry admixture. Jomon ancestry, estimated using the Jomon allele score (JAS), was associated with clinical measures, including renal-related traits and serum triglycerides in 34,152 Tohoku Medical Megabank participants. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics of donors from the upper and lower extremes of the JAS distribution (n = 10) suggested group-level differences in immune-related gene expression. To test whether the serum triglyceride association coincided with hepatic cellular phenotypes, we differentiated hiPSCs from these donors into hepatocyte-like cells. Neither intracellular triglycerides nor lipid-related gene expression differed between groups. These findings highlight the value of a genetically characterized hiPSC-based framework for investigating ancestry-associated phenotypes across cellular contexts.

title: Cromosomal genomes assemblies of twelve sheep breeds
authors: ECHE, C.; Birdes, C.; Marcuzzo, C.; Sarry, J.; Suin, A.; Vernette, C.; Kuchly, C.; Gaspin, C.; Milan, D.; Donnadieu, C.; Iampietro, C.; Tosser-Klopp, G.; Klopp, C.
abstract: The sheep research community benefits from a genome assembly that has been refined over the last 15 years. However, the rich diversity of sheep breeds suggests that a single individual genome is not enough to represent the species full genomic content. Third-generation sequencing technologies have recently made it possible to generate high quality assemblies that should enable to elucidate unique and/or complex phenotype determinisms depending on genetic structural variations. In the SeqOccin project, twelve breeds were selected to represent (mostly French) sheep genetic diversity: Basco-Bearnaise, Black Belly, Blanche du Massif Central, Corse, Ile de France, Lacaune, Manech Tete Noire, Noire du Velay, Ouessant, Rambouillet, Vendeen, Soay. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from blood samples and subjected to long read whole-genome sequencing. The reads were used to generate de novo assemblies and were aligned onto the public reference to call structural variants. PacBio HiFi and parental Illumina reads were used to assemble phased haplotypes of the Lacaune breed. For the other breeds, PacBio raw (CLR) or ONT reads were generated. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of assembling genomes with a reasonable amount of data and appropriate software packages, delivering one high-quality assembly and 11 standard sheep assemblies that pave the way for pangenome construction and structural variant functional studies.

title: The Genetic Landscape of Structural Variants in Aspergillus flavus using ONT and PacBio Sequencing
authors: Woods, A.; Lohmar, J. M.; Malik, A.; Lustig, A. J.
abstract: Genetic rearrangement in the absence of selection is poorly understood. Long-read, high-depth sequencing has enabled analysis of the genetic landscape of spontaneous structural variants. We have applied PacBio Revio sequencing to identify the major classes of genetic alterations during long-term vegetative growth in Aspergillus flavus. These classes include a) precise deletions frequently associated with the flanking region of homology, b) clusters of short deletions that are heavily enriched within centromeric and subtelomeric regions that are typically 94% A+T, and c) deletions and expansions within a subset of homopolymer tracts. We find 70 homopolymer tracts longer than 44 bp, dispersed throughout the genome in noncoding regions and unassociated with transposable elements. A broader analysis of third-generation sequenced datasets from fungi found within the Phylum Ascomycota showed a high but variable prevalence of homopolymeric tracts across species. The adventitious identification of a putative flbA mutation, responsible for an altered conidial phenotype, by the Deep Variant AI system also demonstrates the power of this approach. These studies show that high-depth, long-read sequencing can probe SNPs, indels, homopolymeric tracts, and large-scale rearrangements in an unbiased fashion, and demonstrate that short deletions and homopolymer tract expansions arise spontaneously in A. flavus and other filamentous fungi.

title: GenDiMug: a generic inclusive multigraph framework to analyze genomic organizations and -omics data at multiple scales
authors: Teuliere, J.; Lopez, P.; Corel, E.; Llorente, B.; Bapteste, E.
abstract: After decades of investigation, analyses of genome organization remain challenging. This is because genome descriptions are very information-rich and usually rendered as a linear map of genomic features corresponding to an ordered list of position intervals on a nucleic acid macromolecular backbone. This formalism, while accurate, is not fully optimized to mathematically analyze all genome structural properties, in particular the relations between genomic features, nor to integrate large amounts of -omics data, such as transcriptomes, epigenomes, proteomes, meltomes or chromatin accessibility data, which are increasingly available. We therefore developed GenDiMug, a tool that uses a network representation of the genome as a backbone, providing a natural framework to integrate spatial and ontogenetic relationships between genomic features and multi-omics data. We illustrate how this generic approach can be applied to all sorts of genomes, both to visualize genomic topology at contig and chromosomal scales at base-pair resolution, and to analyze genome positional effects using various graph metrics. Using GenDiMug, we further reveal clumping of genes with similar expression levels in eukaryotic genomes and their possible circadian regulation in a photosynthetic alga.

title: Inferring ecDNA Evolution from Allele Frequency Spectra
authors: Dameracharla, B.; Prasad, G.; Luebeck, J.; Amin, S.; Kirkland, J.; Chapman, O. S.; Chavez, L.; Verhaak, R.; Huang, W.; Mischel, P. S.; Werner, B.; Bafna, V.
abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) can arise early in the development of aggressive tumors or later upon progression, but the impact of chronology on patient outcome is not known. Currently, it is not possible to determine when an ecDNA arose in the course of tumor development and progression, based on genome sequencing data. Here, we develop an analytic method, ecEvol, to infer ecDNA emergence time, selection strength, mutation rate, and clonal dominance from allele frequency spectra in bulk whole-genome sequencing. EcEvol outperforms other methods and predicts parameters with high accuracy across a wide range of parameter values. Applying ecEvol to primary, treatment-naive tumors, we find that ecDNA typically emerges early and undergoes strong positive selection, albeit with substantial variation across cancer types. EcDNAs carrying known oncogenes emerge earlier and reach greater clonal dominance than ecDNAs lacking known oncogenes. In advanced and predominantly treated tumors, ecDNA emerges substantially later than in matched primary tumors, consistent with the generation and selection of new ecDNA during tumor progression and therapy. Longitudinal samples further support continued expansion of ecDNA-bearing lineages. Finally, earlier ecDNA emergence is associated with poorer overall survival. These results provide insight into the chronology of ecDNA formation from a single tumor biopsy taken at any point during the course of the disease, revealing that allele-frequency spectra encode the evolutionary history of ecDNA and provide a quantitative framework for reconstructing its emergence and expansion.

title: In silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology approach reveal outer membrane proteins OMP47 and LptD as dual-purpose drug and vaccine targets in Pasteurella multocida Pm70
authors: Khan Chowdhury, A. R.; Islam, S.; Farid, A.; Lamia, F.; Ahmad, T. F.; Hossain, N. J.; Paul, A. R.; Afrin, T.; Elias, S. M.
abstract: Drug targets and vaccines for bacterial diseases are challenging to develop. Computational subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology offer a viable substitute for conventional drug and vaccine development approaches. In recent years, Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative pathogen responsible for severe infections in humans along with major diseases in livestock and poultry, has developed resistance to multiple drugs. As a result, there is an urgent demand for research into reliable, efficient, highly potent, and cost-effective strategies to combat the rise of Pasteurella multocida infections. To address this, the present study integrated an in silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology workflow to pinpoint proteins with potential value as both drug and vaccine targets. From the complete Pasteurella multocida Pm70 proteome, we identified 446 proteins that had no similarities with human proteins, out of which 129 were found to be essential for the pathogens survival. These 129 proteins are therefore potential candidates for drug development. Further metabolic pathway analysis, virulence potential, subcellular localization, and structural analyses revealed two outer membrane proteins, namely, 47 kDa outer membrane protein and lipopolysaccharide-assembly protein LptD, as promising candidates for therapeutic development. Subsequent antigenicity analysis revealed both outer membrane proteins as potential vaccine targets, exhibiting highly favorable antigenicity scores. Candidate B- and T-cell epitopes were systematically mapped from these two targets based on antigenicity, immunogenicity, toxicity, and allergenicity potential and only high-confidence epitopes were assembled using adjuvants and class-specific linkers to construct the final multi-epitope vaccine (MEV). The designed MEV construct was demonstrated to be highly antigenic, non-toxic and non-allergenic to humans, while possessing favorable structural and physicochemical properties, and exhibited strong binding interactions with human toll-like receptors with minimal molecular deformability. Although further experimental validation is recommended to fully assess their efficacy, the present study establishes a solid foundation for the development of novel therapeutics and vaccine candidates against P. multocida, ultimately contributing to the reduction of its rising infections.

title: Version-aware question answering over living oncology guidelines
authors: Ravi Kumar, T.; Kaniyar Narayana Iyengar, A. I.; Khan, M. A.; Khakwani, K. Z. R.; Kathuria, K.; Sonbol, M. B.; Riaz, I.; Gupta, V.
abstract: Living clinical guidelines revise recommendations as evidence emerges, so an AI answer can be faithful to a real guideline and still be out of date. Here we examine this failure using ASCOBench, 288 unique questions in 96 three-turn conversations grounded in versioned American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) breast and prostate cancer guidelines, with oncologist-reviewed reference answers. Oncologists corrected one in four version-sensitive answers drafted by a frontier model, against fewer than one in ten factual ones. Across the guideline corpus, 19 recommendations changed between versions, seven of them reversals, yet only 1 of 14 superseded documents states that it has been replaced. With a strong model, retrieval over several guideline versions made stale answers four times more frequent than answering without retrieval. SentryLine, a verification-first system, lowered incorrect answers to 4.2-5.2% from 9.7-22.9% for baselines across three models. Recognizing change before a guideline declares it remains an open problem.

title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
authors: Emon, M.; Siddiqque, N. H.; Haque, M. E.
abstract: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.

title: Gradients of local circuit architecture shape stability and information integration across the cortical hierarchy
authors: Green, L.; Ito, S.; Haufler, D.; Rozsa, M.; Wang, C.; Daie, K.; Arkhipov, A.
abstract: The mammalian neocortex is a complex structure with many interacting regions and cell types. Multiple efforts have recently generated large datasets from multiple cortical regions to determine generalizing principles of cortical organization and activity. One such generalizing principle is the concept of a cortical hierarchy - low-dimensional macroscopic gradients of biological properties across cortical areas and a hierarchy of timescales for information processing. Such gradients in properties along a cortical hierarchy may explain how different cortical regions serve different computational roles (i.e. sensory processing versus working memory). We set out to investigate such principles using biologically realistic simulations. Starting from our previously published model of the mouse primary visual cortex (VISp) with updated connectivity reflecting recent large-scale connectomics and synaptic physiology datasets, we generated multiple versions of the cortical circuit model with increased connectivity as measured along the cortical hierarchy. We then measure the resulting neural activity in response to a simulated single-cell photostimulation paradigm and thalamocortical inputs. We found that overall circuit stability increased across the cortical hierarchy, due to both increases in connection density and increases in the relative proportion of SST cells. The results of this study link cortical cell types to population-level activity, generating insight into the function of local circuits across cortex.

title: Primate Gaze Behavior Reflects Change of Mind in a Naturalistic Navigation Task
authors: Choi, W.; Alefantis, P.; Andreadakis, G.; Angelaki, D. E.
abstract: Revising a decision while acting on it is a fundamental aspect of natural behavior, yet the underlying computations are difficult to track in real time. To explore how such belief updates unfold, we tested whether eye movements reveal a subject's change of mind during a naturalistic navigation task with a binary target choice. Humans and monkeys were required to navigate to one of two goal locations presented either simultaneously or sequentially in a virtual environment where explicit position cues were absent. Our findings reveal that gaze continuously tracks the latent variable, including changes of mind. We found that the target tracking accuracy before the second target is even presented during sequential target trials predicts whether the subject's navigational goal persists (first target choice) or changes (second target choice). These results underscore the importance of gaze in action planning and changes of mind, supporting the hypothesis that eye movements embody not only the current latent variable but also its uncertainty.

title: Impacts of different SETD1A mutations and genetic backgrounds on human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived hippocampal neurons
authors: Hong, Y.; Zhao, T.; Yang, Q.; Zhang, H.; Ma, X.; Su, X.; Liu, J.; Zhang, S.; Mendez-Maldonado, K.; Zhou, Y.; Zou, J.; Kreimer, A.; Sawa, A.; Christian, K.; Pang, Z.; Duan, J.; Song, H.; Ming, G.-L.
abstract: Abstract Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) provide a translational platform to interrogate the impact of genetic risk factors for various disorders on human biology. It has been a common practice to engineer premature stop codons to model predicted loss-of-function mutations using isogenic hiPSCs, yet effects of mutation position for the same gene and genetic background have been rarely tested systematically and at multiple levels for comparison to those of patient-specific mutations. Ultra-rare, heterozygous, and predicted loss-of-function mutations in the SETD1A gene, which encodes a H3K4 methyltransferase, are highly penetrant genetic risk factors for schizophrenia. Here, we generated a large panel of isogenic heterozygous SETD1A mutant hiPSC lines, including premature stop-codon mutations in one early exon and one late exon in five genetic backgrounds and two patient-specific mutations, to gain insight into molecular, cellular, and functional changes in a disease-relevant and highly pure population of human hippocampal dentate granule cell-like neurons. Our multi-level analyses showed that different SETD1A mutations lead to divergent molecular and cellular phenotypes related to synapses, but convergent neuronal network deficits, while the genetic background influences gene expression with no substantial effects at cellular and network levels. Mechanistic analysis confirmed the early exon patient mutation as loss-of-function, but revealed that the predicted loss-of-function patient mutation in the late exon is likely gain-of-function. Consequently, while all mutations decreased global H3K4me3 levels, deficits were only partially rescued by inhibiting H3K4 demethylase LSD1 for early exon mutations, but not for late exon mutations. Together, these results suggest that highly penetrant mutations can lead to similar cellular and functional phenotypes across different genetic backgrounds, whereas different premature stop-codon mutations could have contrasting impacts due to distinct mechanisms. Our findings have practical implications for applying genome-editing in hiPSCs to model disorders, highlight the value of modeling patient-specific mutations and testing multiple mutations, and suggest the need for tailored mutation-dependent therapeutic strategies.

title: A Hypothalamic Pathway for Energy Conservation
authors: Douglass, A.; Lynch, N.; Andina, M.; Ramirez-Plascencia, O.; Kucukdereli, H.; Melville, D.; Costa, L.; Yang, Y.; Qiu, C.; Bandaru, S.; Banks, A.; Hrvatin, S.; Saper, C.; Lowell, B. B.; Machado, N.
abstract: Many animals utilize a survival strategy of hypothermia, inactivity, and a dramatic decrease in their energy metabolism when faced with a shortfall in energy supplies. Mice, for example, show daily torpor that may last several hours to bridge the lack of energy availability in a cold environment. While our recent studies identified a population of neurons in the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO) necessary for fasting-induced torpor regulation, the specific brain circuits that trigger energy conservation in response to food restriction are unknown. We show here that the energy state of the animal is conveyed to preoptic neurons by inputs from the arcuate nucleus (ARC), a region known to be indispensable for driving metabolic and behavioral adaptations to the fasted state. We first found that the activity of ARC neurons expressing Agouti-Related Peptide (ARCAgRP) is required for the generation of fasting-induced torpor. Then, we showed that torpor-active ARCAgRP neurons innervate the preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA), including the MnPO. Using optogenetic methods, we also found that activating the ARCAgRP-MnPO pathway induces key features of torpor: decreased body temperature, bradycardia, reduction of energy expenditure, and suppression of brown adipose tissue thermogenesis. Remarkably, we also show that inhibition of the ARCAgRP-MnPO brain circuit entirely prevents fasting-induced torpor. Furthermore, we identified that both NPY and GABA are neuromodulators used by ARCAgRP neurons to enable hypothermic responses during starvation. Our studies provide a detailed view of a hypothalamic pathway enabling energy conservation, a survival mechanism in conditions of low energy availability.

title: Plasticity-induced actin polymerization positions endocytic compartments at the bases of stimulated spines
authors: Wong, V. C.; Walpita, D.; Liu, Z. J.; O'Shea, E. K.
abstract: The endocytic pathway plays key roles in facilitating and regulating synaptic plasticity, but how its components are organized at spines undergoing plasticity is not fully understood. Here we use live-cell imaging and single-particle tracking to examine the localization of endosomes and lysosomes in response to plasticity-inducing stimuli. We find that endosomes and lysosomes are positioned and retained near the bases of stimulated spines after the induction of structural plasticity in a manner dependent on actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft. Spines with endocytic compartments near their bases exhibit greater glutamate receptor turnover and more sustained enlargement after stimulation than spines lacking them. These results suggest that actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft acts as a hub to organize critical cellular machinery at the bases of spines undergoing synaptic plasticity.

title: Inflections in adolescent cortical maturation signal psychopathology risk
authors: Clauss, J. A.; Zhi, D.; Perdomo, S. A.; Dear, R.; Kunitoki, K.; Hughes, D. E.; Blum, A. T.; Kane, K. A.; Elyounssi, S.; Cooper, B.; Laurent, E.; Bazer, O.; Vinke, L.; O'Dor, S.; Flook, E. A.; Linnman, C.; Kritzer-Cheren, M. D.; Holt, D. J.; Lee, P. H.; Dunn, E. C.; Lee, H.; Satterthwaite, T. D.; Doyle, A. E.; Barch, D. M.; Gilman, J. M.; Vertes, P. E.; Bullmore, E. T.; Roffman, J. L.
abstract: Cerebral cortical maturation supports emotional, social, and cognitive development during adolescence1. Neurodevelopmental theories of psychiatric illnesses, which peak in onset around age 182, implicate subtle alterations in adolescent cortical development3. However, mechanistic links between cortical maturation and emergent psychopathology have remained elusive. This gap likely reflects a need for more nuanced understanding of cortical development4, larger, longitudinal samples powered to detect small effects,5 and more uniform image quality control.6 Using 29,482 structural MRI scans from 11,720 adolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we demonstrate reproducible differences in the contour and tempo of maturation across the cortical surface. Regional trajectories are robust to image quality variance and align with increasing functional specialization over time. Thicker cortex in early-maturing sensory regions predicts psychiatric symptoms as early as four years prior to their emergence, a pattern that subsequently spreads to association cortex. Overlap with spatially and temporally organized gene co-expression networks implicates prenatal programming of this sequence of maturation and its links to psychopathology. These findings present a novel, versatile neurodevelopmental framework for cortical maturation during adolescence that sequentially implicates sensory and association cortex in risk for emergent psychiatric symptoms.

title: Serum Electrolyte Concentrations Are Associated With Motor Nerve Conduction Velocity in Children
authors: Broser, P. J.
abstract: Axonal action potential propagation critically depends on tightly regulated intra and extracellular electrolyte concentrations and acid base homeostasis. Experimental studies have demonstrated that changes in extracellular sodium, potassium, and calcium concentrations alter axonal excitability and conduction properties. However, it remains unknown whether small variations in electrolyte concentrations within the physiological range are associated with measurable changes in nerve conduction velocity in humans. In this study, data from neurologically healthy children who underwent both nerve conduction studies and blood gas analysis were analyzed to investigate the relationship between electrolyte concentrations and median motor nerve conduction velocity. Nerve conduction velocity was significantly negatively correlated with ionized calcium concentration and positively correlated with sodium concentration, whereas no significant correlation was observed for potassium. In an a priori defined multiple linear regression model, ionized calcium, sodium, and bicarbonate remained significantly associated with nerve conduction velocity after correction for multiple testing. These findings indicate that even small variations in electrolyte concentrations within the physiological range are associated with measurable differences in peripheral nerve conduction velocity and suggest an additional contribution of acid base status to nerve conduction.

title: Neural Dissociation of Cognitive Maps and Graphs in the Human Brain
authors: Xu, Y.; Hinrichs, M. A. B.; Bottini, R.; Doeller, C. F.
abstract: Cognitive maps and graphs offer two distinct ways of organizing knowledge: maps arrange items within a spatial layout, whereas graphs thread them together through experiential transitions. However, spatial proximity and experiential contiguity are typically correlated, and content represented in one format can often be transformed into the other, making their neural representations difficult to disentangle. Here, we orthogonally manipulated Euclidean distance, indexing spatial proximity, and shortest-path distance, indexing experiential contiguity, within the same learned environment. Using fMRI and whole-brain searchlight representational similarity analysis, we identified dissociable representations of these two formats in the human brain. Euclidean distance was represented in the intraparietal sulcus, whereas shortest-path distance was represented in the hippocampal/parahippocampal region and in cortical areas that overlapped substantially with scene-selective regions. ROI analyses further supported the specificity of these representations across regions. Together, these findings provide neural evidence for a dissociation between cognitive maps and cognitive graphs.

title: A neural circuit algorithm for action grammar
authors: Liu, Y.; Tian, L. Y.; Tenenbaum, J. B.; Freiwald, W. A.; Wang, X.-J.
abstract: How does the brain generate sequences of discrete elements, such as actions or words, that follow an abstract rule (a grammar)? Motivated by an experiment in which monkeys learned to draw multi-object images according to grammatical rules, we trained a recurrent neural network to generate sequences Am Bn: producing shape A m times, then B n times, or vice versa. Our findings are threefold. First, the network plans the sequence by moving to an initial state encoding m and n along orthogonal directions for upcoming execution. Second, the network repeats each shape by progressing along a shape-specific manifold. Third, transitions from Am to Bn follow parallel trajectories between manifolds across values of n, thus preserving n. Each of these is an experimentally testable prediction. The network generalizes to longer novel sequences by starting further along the same orthogonal directions. These results reveal a neural circuit implementation of a symbolic algorithm for generating rule-based action sequences.

title: Cortical projection neurons exhibit early maturation defects and selective degeneration in a mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy
authors: Schellino, R.; La Rocca, F.; Iezzi, G.; Caretto, A.; Boido, M.; Vercelli, A.
abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is usually considered a lower motor neuron disease; however, growing evidence from both experimental models and clinical studies indicates that SMN deficiency affects the whole CNS, beyond the spinal and brainstem motor system. Here, we investigated the temporal progression and selective vulnerability of cortical projection neurons in the SMN{Delta}7 mouse model at early (P5) and late (P11) symptomatic stages. Combining subtype-specific immunohistochemistry, DiI tracing associated with morphometric reconstruction, and dendritic spine analysis, we identified stage- and subtype-dependent cortical alterations. At P11, corticospinal and infragranular callosal projection neurons were selectively reduced in number and showed marked dendritic remodeling and altered excitatory synaptic organization, whereas corticothalamic neurons and supragranular SATB2-positive populations were comparatively preserved. Notably, cortical abnormalities were already detectable at P5, before overt neuronal loss: indeed, corticospinal neurons exhibited reduced soma size and dendritic complexity, while dendritic spine density remained preserved, but spine morphology was shifted toward immature phenotypes. These early maturation defects persisted during disease progression and preceded the reduction in spine density observed at P11. Together, our findings identify cortical projection neurons as selectively vulnerable to constitutive SMN deficiency and suggest that impaired neuronal and synaptic maturation represents an early feature of cortical pathology preceding subtype-specific neurodegeneration. These results expand the pathophysiological spectrum of SMA beyond lower motor neurons and highlight early brain alterations as a potential component of disease progression.

title: ATP1A3 dysfunction alters excitability and developmental trajectory of human neurons in alternating hemiplegia of childhood
authors: Thompson, C. H.; Simmons, C. Q.; Wafa, S. A.; George, A. L.
abstract: Pathogenic variants in ATP1A3, encoding the neuronal Na/K-ATPase, are associated with a spectrum of neuro-developmental disorders including alternating hemiplegia of childhood (AHC). ATP1A3 is expressed throughout the cortex during early development, and later becomes enriched in GABAergic neurons. Here, we interrogated the underlying mechanisms and neurophysiological consequences of a recurrent AHC-associated variant (ATP1A3-G947R) in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) derived glutamatergic and GABAergic neu-rons. We found that glutamatergic and GABAergic AHC neurons exhibited smaller ouabain-sensitive pump cur-rents compared to isogenic mutation-corrected control neurons. This impairment of pump function correlated with a depolarized potassium reversal potential, lower intracellular potassium concentration, and depolarized resting membrane potential for both cell types compared to isogenic control neurons. Additionally, using a Na+ sensitive dye, we observed that AHC neurons had a higher basal intracellular Na+ concentration that recovered more slowly following Na+ loading compared to isogenic control neurons. As an additional consequence of impaired pump function and abnormal Na+ dynamics, glutamatergic and GABAergic AHC neurons were more prone to depolarization block. Finally, the time course by which GABA neurotransmission switches from excita-tory to inhibitory was delayed in glutamatergic AHC neurons compared to isogenic controls. Our findings pro-vide evidence that impairment of ATP1A3 function has direct effects on ionic homeostasis, leading to cascading effects on intrinsic neuronal firing and maturation of GABAergic neurotransmission that advance understanding of the pathophysiology of AHC.

title: An astrocytic AMPAR-dependent parity signal preserves synaptic strength
authors: Elazar, N.; Ravenel, J. R.; Kim, J.; Vaidyanathan, T.; Wirfel-Farenchak, O.; Uryu, K.; Lim, S. S. X.; Roach, J. R.; Zhang, W.; Cao, X.; van Praag, M. E.; Yan, H.; Yu, G.; Tadross, M. R.; Eroglu, C.
abstract: Astrocytic processes closely associate with excitatory synapses and express AMPARs, positioning them to sense the same glutamate signals as neurons. Whether a mismatch between neuronal and astrocytic glutamate sensing affects synaptic physiology is unknown. Using AstroHTP, an extension of Drug Acutely Restricted by Tethering (DART) for cell-type-specific pharmacology, we found that acute astrocytic AMPAR inhibition spared neuronal AMPARs and basal transmission yet converted ongoing glutamatergic activity into a remarkably potent form of long-term depression (LTD) in mouse striatal projection neurons (SPNs). Unlike canonical presynaptic LTD, this form of LTD manifests postsynaptically, requires non-ionotropic NMDA receptor signaling, and arises when glutamate transmission occurs without a matching astrocytic signal. Astrocytic glutamate sensing through AMPARs, therefore, acts as a parity signal that verifies transmission and stabilizes active synapses.

title: A touch that lingers: synchronized patting strengthens neural tracking of auditory rhythm in newborns
authors: Hegde, M.; Edalati, M.; Kosem, A.; Foulon, A.; Lefebvre, S.; Wallois, F.; Trainor, L.; Tillmann, B.; Moghimi, S.
abstract: Rhythmic auditory stimulation in early life rarely occurs in isolation. Caregivers naturally combine singing and speech with rhythmic touch, rocking, and visual cues. Newborns are sensitive to auditory rhythm from birth, yet little is known about how temporally aligned information across sensory modalities shapes the neural encoding of auditory rhythmic structure. Here, we tested whether rhythmic touch can alter how the newborn brain tracks an ongoing auditory signal beyond the period of tactile stimulation. We recorded high-density electroencephalography from full-term newborns (N = 40), 1-3 days after birth, while they were exposed to recorded French lullabies presented either alone or accompanied by gentle patting synchronized with the metrically strong beat. Patting was delivered intermittently, allowing us to compare neural responses to lullabies across conditions, notably during periods without concurrent tactile stimulation. We quantified neural tracking of the lullabies using brain-stimulus coherence and temporal response function modeling. Newborns' neural activity synchronized with the rhythmic structure of the lullabies at frequencies corresponding to both the beat and the metrically accented strong beat. Critically, neural tracking was stronger when the lullabies had been accompanied by synchronized touch than when they were presented alone, and this enhancement persisted during subsequent periods in which no touch was delivered. Although rhythmic touch enhanced tracking in newborns with both weaker and stronger auditory-only tracking, there was a larger gain in those who initially showed weaker auditory tracking. Together, our findings reveal that the newborn brain exploits rhythmic touch to strengthen its encoding of auditory rhythm, and that this benefit outlasts the touch itself. This provides neural evidence that patting an infant in time with a song, a caregiving practice shared across cultures, does more than simply provide a tactile stimulation. It shapes how the newborn brain encodes the song's rhythm.

title: A gut-brain microbial sensing pathway mediates host defense and bacterial clearance
authors: Runyon, A.; Zhang, P.; Ye, L.
abstract: The digestive tract is a major site of nutrient absorption. It also harbors the densest microbial communities in our body. It is well known that the brain perceives ingested nutrient information through the intestinal epithelium enteroendocrine cell (EEC)-vagal pathway. Little is known about how the brain senses gut bacteria that reside in the intestinal lumen. In this study, we combined novel in vivo EEC calcium imaging, EEC optochemical stimulation, and vagal sensory neuron calcium imaging in the zebrafish model, and revealed that segregated pathways mediated by different EEC and vagal sensory neuron subtypes differentially perceive beneficial nutrient information and harmful irritant pathogenic bacterial information. Our study revealed that a group of EECs that express the nociceptive receptor Transient receptor potential ankyrin A1 (Trpa1) can be activated by the pathogenic bacterium Edwardsiella tarda (E. tarda) or E. tarda-produced irritant metabolites. These Trpa1+EECs do not sense nutrients. Trpa1+EECs, but not other EECs, uniquely and highly express both Serotonin and the neuronal peptide Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (Pacap). Using pharmaceutical and genetic approaches, our data showed that Pacap synergizes with Serotonin and is required for Trpa1+EEC-induced vagal activation. Stimulating the Trpa1+EEC-vagal sensory pathway potently inhibits a group of vagal motor neurons that innervate visceral organs in the caudal dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (cDMV). However, the same group of cDMV neurons is activated by nutrients. Microbially induced cDMV inhibition enhances liver gluconeogenesis and promotes intestinal neutrophil recruitment. Inhibiting glucose metabolism, disrupting Trpa1+EEC-vagal sensory pathway, or optogenetically activating cDMV neurons in E. tarda colonized zebrafish induces intestinal E. tarda to switch from an aggregated phenotype to a diffused phenotype and hinders E. tarda clearance. Furthermore, our data show that disrupting the Trpa1+EEC-vagal sensory pathway impairs intestinal neutrophil recruitment and hinders survival, suggesting a protective role of the Trpa1+EEC-vagal microbial sensing pathway in pathogen defense. Together, our data revealed that a distinct non-nutrient-sensing Trpa1+EEC-vagal circuit senses gut microbial irritants, coordinating neuronal, metabolic, and immune responses to enhance host defense and pathogen clearance.

title: A low-adhesion mechanism enables axon growth in the developing brain
authors: Alfadil, E.; Filser, S.; Escribano, B.; Bradke, F.
abstract: During development, axons grow through complex tissue environments to wire the brain. Axon growth speeds measured in cell culture are incompatible with the distances axons must cover in vivo. Yet how axons achieve the growth speeds required to establish long-range connectivity within a narrow embryonic developmental window, and by what mechanism, remains unknown. Here, using long-term live imaging in brain sections, mouse genetics, molecular and pharmacological perturbations, together with AxoVivo, a newly developed intravital imaging platform that resolves subcellular structures, including growth cones and cytoskeletal dynamics, in living mouse embryos, we show that axons of cortical projection neurons (CPNs) employ a low-adhesion mechanism to grow. Even as growth cones change shape and turn, axons grow an order of magnitude faster than in vitro. The actin motor myosin II controls the growth cone actin cytoskeleton and its morphology but not axon growth itself, which is instead promoted by microtubule stabilisation. Finally, super-resolution shadow imaging (SUSHI) revealed that growth cones do not pull on the surrounding extracellular matrix. Taken together, this low-adhesion mechanism driven by protruding microtubules ensures the rapid growth necessary for long-distance wiring of the developing nervous system.

title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
authors: Deb, S.; Bhunia, D.; Singh, V. A.; Muralidharan, V.; Roy, D.
abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF +/- 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

title: Genome-engineered C. elegans strains with sex-transformed neurons and gut
authors: Liao, C.-P.; Ji, H.; Hobert, O.
abstract: The sexual identity of specific tissues can be altered through cell-autonomous manipulation of the sex determination pathway in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Previously described sexually mosaic strains carried multicopy transgenic arrays that are potentially subject to transgene silencing or misexpression artefacts. We used here the CRISPR/Cas9 system to engineer strains in which coding sequences for either a masculinizing agent (FEM-3) or a feminizing agent (intracellular domain of TRA-2) are inserted with a trans-splicing system at the 3 end of endogenous genetic loci that are known to be expressed in either a neuron-specific (rab-3) or gut-specific (elt-2) manner. We validate the tissue-specific sex-transformations induced by these genomic manipulations through expression analysis of known sex-specific genes and through assaying behavioral readouts. These strains may serve the worm community as standard reference tools to study the consequences of tissue-specific sex transformations.

title: Ultrastructurally planar growth cones during neocortical axon navigation
authors: Nakanishi, Y.; Tsuboi, M.; Kawai, H.; Shibayama, K.; Yamauchi, K.; Looprasertkul, S.; Lee, K.; Komaki, H.; Egashira, T.; Suga, S.; Murakami, T.; Ohki, K.; Hioki, H.; Ohno, N.; Mizuno, H.; Hirabayashi, Y.
abstract: Neurons extend axons toward spatially defined but often distant targets to establish brain circuits. Callosal projection neurons exemplify this organization, linking corresponding cortical territories between the two hemispheres. Growing axons rely on growth cones to regulate direction and speed through densely packed tissues. Although growth cone morphology and dynamics have been extensively characterized in cultured neurons and invertebrate models, how growth cones navigate the three-dimensional environment of the developing mammalian brain remains poorly explored. Here, we combined a genetically encoded electron microscopy (EM)-labeling strategy and zero-shot deep-learning-based tracing with high-resolution volume EM to reconstruct growth cones of identified callosal projection neurons in the developing mouse brain. Mediolaterally extending growth cones exhibited a planar, fan-shaped morphology, preferentially expanded along the dorsoventral axis. Filopodia extended from the edges of this plane and aligned predominantly with the same axis but showed no directional bias toward the growing direction. Longitudinal in vivo imaging revealed that increased growth cone complexity associated with filopodial extension coincided with lower instantaneous velocity but preceded accelerated extension. Together, these findings reveal a dorsoventrally oriented planar growth cone architecture in which filopodial extension precedes accelerated axon growth, suggesting a structural constraint that may restrict axon navigation to the callosal plane.
